== Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:531-660

\section{Declarations with Static Parameters}
\seclabel{overloading-static-params}

The rules above compare the parameter types and the return types of
declarations without static parameters.
A declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose parameter
type ranges over every instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their
bounds (\secref{overloading-terms}).
A declaration $d_1$ is more specific than a declaration $d_2$ when $d_2$ is
applicable to every call to which $d_1$ is applicable, and not the other way
round (\secref{resolving-overloading}); where neither has static parameters,
this is the relation $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$ of the rules above.
A set of overloaded declarations, some or all of which have static parameters,
is a valid overloading when every pair $d_1$, $d_2$ of them satisfies the
following three rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The \emph{No Duplicates Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each applicable to every
call to which the other is applicable.
\item
The \emph{Meet Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ exclude each other, or one of them is more
specific than the other, or some declaration of the set is more specific than
both and applicable to every call to which both are applicable.
\item
The \emph{Return Type Rule}: if $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$, then for
every argument type other than \TYP{BottomType} to which $d_1$ is applicable,
and for every instance of $d_2$ that is applicable to it, some instance of $d_1$
is applicable to it whose return type is a subtype of the return type of that
instance of $d_2$.
\end{itemize}
\revision{revival-overloading}{The revival's text of 30~September 2026 stated
the No Duplicates Rule as ``$d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each more specific than the
other'', which the strict sense of more specific above made refuse no pair.
It is stated on the relation without ``and not the other way round'', as the
type group's papers of 2011 and 2019 state it, and so it refuses
\EXP{\VAR{dup}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{Box}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket)}
beside \EXP{\VAR{dup}\llbracket{}U\rrbracket(x\COLON
\TYP{Box}\llbracket{}U\rrbracket)}, each applicable to every call to which the
other is.}
The Subtype Rule, the Incompatibility Rule and the Meet Rule above are these
rules for declarations without static parameters, with the conditions that
coercion adds; the Return Type Rule is the Subtype Rule's condition on return
types, checked over every instance of the less specific declaration and not
over one instance chosen for the pair.

As in \secref{more-specific-rule}, declarations of the set that are each more
specific than both $d_1$ and $d_2$ and that together cover every argument to
which both are applicable also satisfy the Meet Rule.
\revision{revival-meet}{The type group's paper of 2011 states the Meet Rule
without this case.}

Two parameter types with static parameters exclude each other, for the Meet
Rule and the Incompatibility Rule, as the type group's paper of 2011 decides it
by \emph{existential reduction}: each static parameter stands for any type
within its bound, and where the two parameter types mention one parameterized
trait, instantiation exclusion (\secref{trait-types}) lets them meet only where
the static arguments of those mentions are the same, every static argument but
an operator argument counting.
So where \TYP{Box} and \TYP{Pair} are distinct object types with static
parameters, the parameter types \EXP{\TYP{Box}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} and
\EXP{\TYP{Pair}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket} of two declarations exclude each
other whatever \VAR{T}, \VAR{A} and \VAR{B} stand for.

The Return Type Rule refuses the following pair, where trait \TYP{Round}
extends trait \TYP{Shape} and object \TYP{Circle} extends \TYP{Round}:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T = x
%ident(x: Round): Round = x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}(x\COLON \TYP{Round})\COLON \TYP{Round} = x\)
\end{Fortress}
The second declaration is more specific than the first.
For an argument of type \TYP{Circle}, the instance of the first at \TYP{Circle}
is applicable and returns a \TYP{Circle}, but the second, which runs for such an
argument, returns only a \TYP{Round}, and it has no other instance.
The pair is allowed when the second declaration is itself generic:
%ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T = x
%ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T = x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Round}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)
\end{Fortress}
Its instance at any type to which it is applicable returns that type.
\revision{revival-overloading}{This section is new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 required overloaded declarations to have
identical static parameters and ignored them.
The rules stated are those of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn,
Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple
Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011),
which the compiled type checker applies, with its Return Type Rule checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; the pair refused above has the
shape of that paper's own example, which the compiled path used to accept and
then fail to verify.
Neither implementation runs the pair allowed above today: the interpreter
refuses it at load, since it asks two declarations with static
parameters for a pair of parameter types that exclude each other (row~159 of the
revival's gap ledger), and the compiled code generator fails on it (row~537).
The compiled implementation adds one restriction that is not a rule of the
language.
When one declaration with static parameters is more specific than another that
declares as many static parameters of its own, the two must declare them of the
same kinds, position by position, and the return type of the more specific one
must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are identified
position by position; for its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
by position, to whichever declaration the call dispatches to (row~398 of the
revival's gap ledger).
So it refuses this override, whose return type names its static parameters in
the other order, where \TYP{Pr} is an object with two type parameters:
%trait Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\A, B\]
%end
%object M extends Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\B, A\] = Pr[\B, A\](1)
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Maker}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{make}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket()\COLON \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object} M \KWD{extends} \TYP{Maker}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{make}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket()\COLON \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}B, A\rrbracket = \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}B, A\rrbracket(1)\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
The type group's paper of 2019 (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019)
instantiates a dispatched declaration from the dynamic types of the arguments
and the static type of the call, renaming static parameters freely
(\secref{resolving-overloading}); under it the override is valid, and the
restriction goes when the compiled dispatcher instantiates a declaration that
way.}

== Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:259-529

\section{Meet Rule}
\seclabel{more-specific-rule}

If neither the Subtype Rule nor the Incompatibility Rule holds 
for a pair of overloaded declarations 
then the declarations introduce the possibility of ambiguity.  
To avoid this ambiguity, 
we require a \emph{disambiguating declaration}:
for any possible arguments to which both declarations are applicable, 
there must be another more specific declaration that is also applicable.  
Thus, 
if the functional is called with such arguments, 
neither of the pair of declarations is executed 
because the disambiguating declaration is also applicable, 
and it is more specific than both.

\note{What is "an intersection of two declarations"?
-- Sukyoung

For function declarations we require that the disambiguating
declaration be the intersection of the pair of overloaded
declarations.}

\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Functions:}
Suppose that $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are two function
declarations in a single scope
such that neither $\Ps$ nor $\Qs$ is a subtype of the other and $\Ps$ and
$\Qs$ are not incompatible with one another.
Let $\mathpzc{S}$ be the set of types that $\Ps$ defines coercions from
and $\mathpzc{T}$ be the set of types that $\Qs$ defines coercions from.
$\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid overloading if
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ in the scope.

all of the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter
\Qs)$ in the scope,
and
\item
either $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$ or $\Qs \morespecific \Ps$ or for all
$\Ps' \in \mathpzc{S}$ and $\Qs' \in \mathpzc{T}$ one of the two
conditions holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$\Ps' \excludes \Qs'$, or
\item
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps' \inter \Qs')$ in the scope.
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Where the Meet Rule for functions asks for a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ in
the scope, it is also satisfied by declarations in the scope whose parameter
types are each a subtype of both $\Ps$ and $\Qs$ and together cover
$\Ps \inter \Qs$ (\secref{internal-types}): every value of both $\Ps$ and $\Qs$
is a value of the parameter type of one of them, for every value a program can
make, not only for the values a program does make.
Each such declaration is more specific than both $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$, and
at run time it is applicable to every argument whose value its parameter type
holds.
Every pair of the covering declarations must satisfy the overloading rules in
turn, as every pair of the set must.
This case does not apply to the condition on the types from which $\Ps$ and
$\Qs$ define coercions: covering does not choose between two coercions.
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 asked for a
declaration on the intersection itself, and the draft note above asked what the
intersection of two declarations is.
The answer is the one the team's list of proposed features records for two
traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses, ``We agreed to revise the Meet rule to
address this with the coverage check''.
It is an addition to the Meet Rule of the type group's paper of 2011, which asks
for a declaration on the meet; the paper of 2019 has no traits with
\KWD{comprises} clauses.
Where a trait with static parameters stands between two traits with
\KWD{comprises} clauses and their listed types, the intersection of the two is
not equal to a named type (\secref{internal-types}), and only declarations that
together cover it can disambiguate them.
The coverage is a judgement of the overloading rules alone: it makes no type a
subtype of another (row~492 of the revival's gap ledger).}

Recall that $\Ps \inter \Qs$ is the intersection of types $\Ps$ and $\Qs$
as defined in \secref{internal-types}.
We write $\Ps \inter \Qs$ to denote the intersection of types $\Ps$ and $\Qs$.
If for some type $S$ we have $S \Ovrsubtype P$ and $S \Ovrsubtype Q$ then
$S \Ovrsubtype (P \intersect Q)$, but it is not necessarily the
case that $S = (P \intersect Q)$ since another type may be more
specific than both $P$ and $Q$.
\label{adv-over-comprises}
For example, suppose the following:
%trait S comprises {U,V} end
%trait T comprises {V,W} end
%trait U extends S excludes W end
%trait V extends {S,T} end
%trait W extends T end
%
%f(s:S) = 1
%f(t:T) = 1
%f(v:V) = 1
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} S \KWD{comprises} \{U,V\} \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} T \KWD{comprises} \{V,W\} \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} U \KWD{extends} S \KWD{excludes} W \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} V \KWD{extends} \{S,T\} \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} W \KWD{extends} T \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(f(s\COLONOP{}S) = 1\)\\
\(f(t\COLONOP{}T) = 1\)\\
\(f(v\COLONOP{}V) = 1\)
\end{Fortress}
Because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
clause of $U$, any value of both $S$ and $T$ is a value of
$V$.  Thus, $V$ covers $S \inter T$, and the declaration $f(V)$
``disambiguates'' $f(S)$ and $f(T)$, i.e., it is applicable to and more
specific for any call at run time to which both $f(S)$ and $f(T)$ are
applicable.
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 concluded that any
subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of $V$, so that $V = S \inter T$.
That holds of types only while no type stands between $S$ or $T$ and their
listed types; a trait with static parameters may (\secref{trait-decls}), and a
static call whose argument has such a type has $f(S)$ and $f(T)$ applicable and
$f(V)$ not.
It runs $f(V)$, and its type is given in
\secref{overloading-coercion-resolution}.}

The Meet Rule shall not be difficult to obey, especially because
the compiler can give useful feedback.  For example:

%  foo(x:Number, y:ZZ64) = ...
%  foo(x:ZZ64, y:Number) = ...
\begin{Fortress}
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{foo}(x\COLONOP\TYP{Number}, y\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = \ldots\)\\
\(  \VAR{foo}(x\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64, y\COLONOP\TYP{Number}) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\end{Fortress}

Assuming that \(\hbox{\ZZ64} \prec \hbox{\TYP{Number}}\), the compiler
reports that these two declarations are a problem because of ambiguity
and suggests that a new declaration for \EXP{\VAR{foo}({\ZZ64},
{\ZZ64})} would resolve the ambiguity. As another example, consider:

% bar(x:Printable) = ...
% bar(x:Throwable) = ...
\begin{Fortress}
{\tt~}\pushtabs\=\+\( \VAR{bar}(x\COLONOP\TYP{Printable}) = \ldots\)\\
\( \VAR{bar}(x\COLONOP\TYP{Throwable}) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\end{Fortress}

Assuming that $\hbox{\TYP{Printable}}$ and $\hbox{\TYP{Throwable}}$
are neither comparable by the subtyping relation nor disjoint, the
compiler reports that these two declarations are a problem because
\TYP{Printable} and \TYP{Throwable} are incomparable but possibly
overlapping types.
As a result, these two declarations are statically rejected.

Unlike for functions, the Meet Rule for dotted methods only applies to
dotted methods that are provided by the same trait or object.  This is
possible because two dotted methods are applicable to a given call
$\As_0.f(\As)$ only if they are both provided by the trait or object
$\As_0$.

\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Dotted Methods:}
Suppose that $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ and $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ are two dotted method
declarations provided by a trait or object $C$ such that neither
$(\Ps_0, \Ps)$ nor $(\Qs_0, \Qs)$ is a subtype of the other and $\Ps$
and $\Qs$ are not incompatible with one another.
Let $\mathpzc{S}$ be the set of
types that $\Ps$ defines coercions from and $\mathpzc{T}$ be the set
of types that $\Qs$ defines coercions from.
$\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ and
$\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ are a valid overloading if
there is a declaration $\Rs_0.\f(\Ps
\inter \Qs)$ provided by $C$ with $\Rs_0 \Ovrsubtype (\Ps_0 \inter
\Qs_0)$.

all of the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or there is a declaration $\Rs_0.\f(\Ps
\inter \Qs)$ provided by $C$ with $\Rs_0 \Ovrsubtype (\Ps_0 \inter
\Qs_0)$, and
\item
either $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$ or $\Qs \morespecific \Ps$ or
for all $\Ps' \in \mathpzc{S}$ and
$\Qs' \in \mathpzc{T}$ one of the two conditions holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$\Ps' \excludes \Qs'$, or
\item
there is a declaration $\Rs_0.\f(\Ps' \inter \Qs')$ provided by $C$
with $\Rs_0 \Ovrsubtype (\Ps_0 \inter \Qs_0)$.
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Recall that functional methods can be viewed semantically as top-level
functions, as described in \secref{methods}.  However, treating
functional methods as top-level functions for determining valid
overloading is too restrictive.  In the following example:
\input{\home/advanced/examples/Overloading.tex}
if the functional methods were interpreted as top-level functions then
this program would define two top-level functions with parameter types
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}}.
These declarations would be
statically rejected as
an invalid overloading because there is no
relation between \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}}; another trait
may extend them both without declaring its own version of the
functional method which may lead to an ambiguous call at run time.
However, notice that declaraions are ambiguous only for calls on
arguments that extend both \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}}, and
any type that extends both can include a new declaration that
disambiguates them.  We use this intuition to allow such overloadings.

\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Functional Methods:}
Suppose that $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are two functional method
declarations occurring in trait or object declarations or object expressions
such that neither $\Ps$ nor $\Qs$ is a subtype of the other and $\Ps$ and $\Qs$
are not incompatible with one another.  Let $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$
have self parameters at $i$ and $j$ respectively.
$\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid
overloading if all of the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$i = j$
\item if there exists a trait or object $C$
that provides both $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ then $\Ps \neq \Qs$ and
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ provide by $C$
having self parameter at $i$.
\end{itemize}

Also, let $\mathpzc{S}$ be the set of types that $\Ps$
defines coercions from and $\mathpzc{T}$ be the set of types that
$\Qs$ defines coercions from.  $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid
overloading if all of the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$i = j$
\item
either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or if there exists a trait or object $C$
that provides both $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ then $\Ps \neq \Qs$ and
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ provide by $C$, and
\item
either $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$ or $\Qs \morespecific \Ps$ or
for all $\Ps' \in \mathpzc{S}$ and
$\Qs' \in \mathpzc{T}$ one of the two conditions holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$\Ps' \excludes \Qs'$, or
\item
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps' \inter \Qs')$ provided by $C$.
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

As for functions, where this rule asks for a declaration
$\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ provided by $C$, it is also satisfied by declarations
provided by $C$, having self parameter at $i$, whose parameter types are each a
subtype of both $\Ps$ and $\Qs$ and together cover $\Ps \inter \Qs$; the case
does not apply to the condition on the types from which $\Ps$ and $\Qs$ define
coercions.
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 asked here, as for
functions, for a declaration on the intersection itself.}

Notice that the Meet Rule for functional methods requires the self
parameters of two overloaded declarations to be in the same position.
This requirement guarantees that no ambiguity is caused by the
position of the self parameter.  Two declarations which differ in the
position of the self parameter must satisfy either the Subtype Rule or
the Incompatibility Rule to be a valid overloading.

Functional method declarations can overload with function declaraions.
A valid overloading between a functional method declaration and
a function declaration is
determined by applying the (more restrictive) Meet Rule for functions
to both declarations.

A trait declaration contains a set of method declarations.
Syntactically, a method declaration begins with
an optional sequence of modifiers followed by
the method's name,
optional static parameters
(described in \chapref{trait-parameters}),
the value parameter with its (optionally) declared type,
an optional type of a return value,
an optional declaration of thrown checked exceptions
(discussed in \chapref{exceptions}),
an optional \KWD{where} clause
(discussed in \secref{where-clauses}),
a contract for the method (discussed in \secref{method-contracts}),
and finally an optional body expression preceded by the token \EXP{=}.
If a method declaration has the \KWD{getter} modifier,
it does not affect the behavior of a program; rather,
it documents that the method is intended to serve as a getter.
A \KWD{throws} clause does not include naked type variables.
Every element in a \KWD{throws} clause is a subtype of
\TYP{CheckedException}.


Method declarations can include the following special modifiers:
\paragraph{\KWD{getter}:}
A method declaration with the modifier \KWD{getter} explicitly declares a
getter method for a field, even in the absence of an actual field declaration.
\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}
If such a field exists, there is no implicit getter for the field.
An explicitly declared getter method must take no arguments and return a
result of the field's type.
A getter method must not throw any checked exception.
Getter names may not overlap ordinary method names.
A getter method must be invoked with the field access syntax:
%expr.id
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{expr}.\VAR{id}\)
\end{Fortress}
where \VAR{id} is the name of the getter method.



\paragraph{\KWD{setter}:}
A method declaration with the modifier \KWD{setter} explicitly declares a
setter method for a field, even in the absence of an actual field.
\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}
If such a field exists, there is no implicit setter for the field.
An explicitly declared setter method must take a single argument---the
value being set---and return \EXP{()}.
A setter method must not throw any checked exception.
Setter names may not overlap ordinary method names.
A setter method must be invoked with the \emph{assignment syntax}:
%expr1.id := expr2
\begin{Fortress}
\({expr}_{1}.\VAR{id} \ASSIGN {expr}_{2}\)
\end{Fortress}


We say that a method declaration \emph{occurs} in a trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{declares} a method declaration that occurs
in that trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{inherits} method declarations from the
declarations of its immediate supertraits
except those method declarations
that are \emph{overridden} (as described later in this section) or
whose parameter type (not including the type of the self parameter)
is equal to the parameter type of a method declaration
that occurs in the trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{provides} the method declarations that it
declares or inherits.




There are two sorts of method declarations:
\emph{dotted method} declarations and
\emph{functional method} declarations.
Syntactically, a dotted method declaration is identical to a function
declaration.
When a method is invoked, a special self parameter is bound to the
object on which it is invoked.



A functional method declaration has a parameter named \KWD{self} at an
arbitrary position in its parameter list.  This parameter is not given a type
and implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object.
\revision{revival-self-type}{In a trait \VAR{T} with a self-type parameter \VAR{X}
(\secref{trait-decls}), this remains the type of the \KWD{self} parameter
in the declaration's signature, which overloading and the choice of a declaration
at a call read; in the method's body \KWD{self} has the type \EXP{T \cap X}
(\secref{idn-ref}).}

\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.b.tex}

\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.c.tex}
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.d.tex}
where \VAR{internalF} is a freshly generated name.
Functional method declarations may be overloaded with top-level function
declarations.
An abstract function declaration
(described in \secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations})
can be provided also for overloaded functional method declarations.

== Specification/basic/traits.tex:413-681

When a method declaration includes a body expression, it is called a
\emph{method definition}.
A method declaration that does not have its body expression is referred to
as an \emph{abstract method declaration}.
An abstract method declaration declares an \emph{abstract method};
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method: a method definition with the same name and the self parameter (if any)
at the same position whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self
parameter, is that of the abstract method declaration, or definitions whose
parameter types are subtypes of it and together cover it
(\secref{internal-types}), or it is a static error.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said only that
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method.
The object defines the method by a body at its parameter type, or by bodies at
narrower parameter types that together cover it, \KWD{comprises} clauses read
at the level of values (\secref{trait-decls}), as
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} asks of the concrete declarations for an
abstract function declaration; one body at a narrower parameter type that does
not cover the abstract method's does not define it.
This is the rule of the type group's compiled type checker (2012) and of its
calculus Welterweight Fortress (2012).
The requirement of \secref{object-decls} that an object define all abstract
methods inherited from its supertraits is unchanged: it defines them in this
sense.}
An abstract method declaration may include the modifier \KWD{abstract}.
It may elide parameter names but parameter
types cannot be omitted except for the self parameter.


\note{
Method declarations that are overridden by some declaration are not
accessible.  They are not considered for overloading checks.

Partial overriding of an overloaded functional is allowed
but partial overriding of a functional declaration is not allowed.
}

A method declaration may have the modifier \KWD{override}.
Such a declaration \emph{overrides} any inherited declaration with the same name
and the self parameter (if any) at the same position,
whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self parameter,
is a strict subtype of the overriding declaration's parameter type.
The return type of the overriding declaration must be subtype of
that of the overridden declaration to preserve type safety.
A declaration with the modifier \KWD{override} must override
some inherited declaration.
It is a static error if a declaration with the modifier \KWD{override}
does not override any inherited declaration.

Here is an example trait \TYP{Enzyme} which provides methods
\VAR{reactionSpeed} and \VAR{catalyze}:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.e.tex}
\TYP{Enzyme}
inherits the abstract method \VAR{mass} from \TYP{OrganicMolecule},
declares the abstract method \VAR{reactionSpeed}, and
declares the concrete method \VAR{catalyze}
which is inherited as an abstract method
from its supertrait \TYP{Catalyst}.

== Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2474-2692

\subsection{Overloading with static parameters}
\seclabel{revival-overloading}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{overloading-terms};
\secref{functional-applicability}; \secref{dotted-method-applicability};
\secref{resolving-overloading}; \secref{principles-overloading};
\secref{overloading-static-params}; \secref{resolving-coercion}; and, in a
draft build, the proposed features of the appendix ``Internal Document''.
\item[Change] The sentence of \secref{overloading-terms} that declarations of
one name may not differ in their static parameters, and its echo in
\secref{principles-overloading}, are replaced: declarations of one name may have
different static parameters, or some of them static parameters and others none,
and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose
parameter type ranges over its instances.
Such a declaration is applicable to a call when some instance of it within its
bounds is, and it is compared with others on the parameter types they declare,
taken over all their instances; the static arguments that a call does not write
are inferred for the declaration it selects, after the selection
(\chapref{type-inference}).
The three sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} that inferred static
parameters before applicability was checked and before declarations were
compared, and the chapter's assumption that the static variables of a call have
been instantiated or inferred, are rewritten to match.
A new section, \secref{overloading-static-params}, states for declarations with
static parameters the three rules of the type group's paper of 2011, the No
Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule, the last checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; how two parameter types with
static parameters exclude each other, by existential reduction with
instantiation exclusion; and a pair that the Return Type Rule refuses, in the
shape of that paper's own example, beside the pair that repairs it.
A box in that section states the restriction that the compiled implementation
adds, that of two declarations with as many static parameters of their own, one
of which is more specific than the other, the two agree on their static
parameters position by position, with an override that reorders them as its
example.
A later revision states the section's No Duplicates Rule on the relation without
``and not the other way round'', that $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each applicable to
every call to which the other is applicable, with a box, and the box on Jan's
example in the internal document gives that rule as its reason.
A further revision has that box say that the factory of \library\ gives a
\TYP{Vector} where its type argument is one of the eight number types and a
plain array where it is any other type, \TYP{Number} among them: the factory
called the vector factory at its own type argument, which has no bound, an
instance that the bound of a \TYP{Vector}'s element type refuses
(\secref{type-param}), and it now builds the vector at each number type, so
that a \TYP{Vector} of \TYP{Number}, which is not well-formed, is no longer its
result.
\secref{resolving-coercion} says in three places that a declaration with static
parameters is applicable when some instance of it is, that it is compared on the
parameter types it declares, and that the declaration selected is then
instantiated, the coercions of its instance inserted statically.
In the internal document, the proposed features on relaxing the restrictions on
the static parameters of overloaded functionals and on overloading with static
parameters are marked done, Jan's example answered by \library's factory and the
questions on exclusion by the existential reduction.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 26~September 2026 that the sentence goes and that this working draft states
the model of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick,
Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple Dispatch
with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011;
\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 132--180, and
\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/setup.tick}, lines 393--397, in the revival's
repository), which the compiled type checker applies, with two changes to the
checker: the Return Type Rule checked over every instance, and the positional
restriction.
On 28~September 2026 it decided that a coercion makes a call possible and never
changes which declaration runs when one is applicable without it, declarations
being chosen on the parameter types they declare and the declaration chosen
being then instantiated.
Neither implementation enforced the sentence: the interpreter has overloaded
declarations with different static parameters since May 2007, the compiled type
checker applies the rules of that paper to them, and \library\ overload across
different static parameters throughout.
The sentence is text of 2009.
The Fortress~1.0 release of 2008 compared generic declarations instead by
using ``their bounds as their supertypes'', in a section whose type relations
``may be replaced when the static type checker and the type inference engine
are implemented'' (\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf},
Section~15.6.1), and the team's unfinished restart of this specification in
2012 dropped the sentence
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/overloading.tick},
lines 100--114, in the revival's repository).
The restart's Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) gives function types that hold
generic and plain declarations together, as sets of arrow types and universal
arrow types, and drops from a quantified type a static parameter that appears
in none of its types
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
553--558, 764--767 and 794--801).
The positional restriction is the compiled implementation's and not the
language's: its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
by position, to whichever declaration dispatch reaches (row~398 of the
revival's gap ledger), while the type group's paper of 2019 instantiates a
dispatched declaration by substitution and renames static parameters freely
(Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, ``Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with
Variance'', POPL 2019, Sections~4 and~5.2).
That paper's soundness proof excludes an upper bound that names a type
parameter, its own included, and closed types, so that \library's families over a type parameter
bounded by an instance of a trait at itself, such as \STR{SUM}, \STR{BIG~MAX}
and those over \TYP{Integral}, rest on the rules of 2011 as the compiled type
checker implements them, and not on the proof of 2019.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
The No Duplicates Rule was first stated on the strict sense of more specific
that the section defines, under which no two declarations are each more
specific than the other, so that it refused no pair, and two declarations each
applicable to every call to which the other is fell to the Meet Rule (row~696
of the revival's gap ledger).
The paper of 2011 defines its relation of specificity without strictness, one
declaration being more specific than another when every type to which the first
is applicable is one to which the second is, and its No Duplicates Rule
``forbids distinct declarations from being equally specific''
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 97--108, 158--162 and 184--185);
the paper of 2019 states it as ``Distinct method declarations must have
different applicable sets'' (Section~2.2), and its rules [No-Dup-Not-Less] and
[No-Dup-Not-Gtr] refuse exactly a pair whose domain types are each a subtype of
the other (Section~4.1 and Figure~5).
The restatement follows the revival's decision of 23~September 2026 that the
type group's later word, that paper among it, outweighs the early text; its
reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] Declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters,
as \library's do.
The compiled type checker refuses the pair of the Return Type Rule's example,
which it accepted before and whose compiled class then failed verification, and
an override whose return type reorders its static parameters, which it accepted
before and which then failed at run time (row~398).
Neither implementation runs every set these rules allow.
The compiled type checker refuses more than the Return Type Rule where the more
specific declaration's parameter type is an object type, as in
\EXP{\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T} beside
\EXP{\VAR{ident}(x\COLON \TYP{Circle})\COLON \TYP{Circle}} where \TYP{Circle} is an
object (row~542); the compiled code generator fails on two declarations with
static parameters whose bounds differ, the pair the Return Type Rule allows in
\secref{overloading-static-params} among them, and on the example of the type
group's paper of 2019 that overloads a method over an array list and a list
(row~537); and the interpreter refuses at load two declarations with static
parameters of which no pair of parameter types excludes each other (row~159),
that example among them (row~539).
Jan's example is still not a valid overloading, its two declarations having the
same parameter type.
The compiled type checker applies the No Duplicates Rule as it is now stated:
it refuses two declarations whose parameter types, read over their instances,
are each a subtype of the other, ``There are multiple declarations of \VAR{dup}
with the same parameter type'', two functional methods among them wherever their
\KWD{self} parameters stand.
It checks no overloading of an operator whose name is not a word of capitals
(row~584 of the revival's gap ledger), and reads no abstract functional method
of a trait that the component it checks declares (row~727): two
declarations of such an operator, or such an abstract method and a concrete
one, with the same parameter type pass it, and only its code generator refuses
them, as a malformed overload set (rows~726 and~727).
The interpreter loads such a pair and runs one of them where both declarations
have static parameters and their parameter types mention one parameterized
type, as \VAR{dup}'s do (row~373), and where one has static parameters and the
other's parameter type is its bound (row~549).
The calculus of \appref{overloading-calculus} keeps its rule that two
declarations with the same number of parameters have static parameters with the
same bounds; it admits fewer overloadings than these chapters, so that its valid
programs are still valid, and its rules and its soundness claim are unchanged
(\secref{revival-calculi}).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/overloading.tex},
lines 100--108:
\begin{quote}
Although there may be multiple declarations with the same functional name,
it is an error for their static parameters to differ (up to
$\alpha$-equivalence), or for one declaration to have static parameters and
another to not have them.
Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which
declarations are applicable, so we ignore them for most of this chapter.
\end{quote}
lines 137--138:
\begin{quote}
We assume throughout this chapter that all static variables in functional calls
have been instantiated or inferred.
\end{quote}
lines 173--175, and in the same words for the types $\Ps_0$ and $\Ps$ of a
dotted method declaration, lines 205--207:
\begin{quote}
If the parameter type $\Ps$ includes static parameters, they are inferred as
described in \chapref{type-inference} before checking the applicability of the
declaration to the call.
\end{quote}
lines 292--295:
\begin{quote}
If the declarations include static parameters, they are inferred as described
in \chapref{type-inference} before comparing their parameter types to determine
which declaration is more specific.
\end{quote}
and \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced/overloading.tex}, lines
95--103:
\begin{quote}
Overloaded declarations must have static parameters that are identical (up to
$\alpha$-equivalence).  Also, valid overloadings for declarations that contain
keyword or varargs parameters are determined by analyzing the expansion of these
declarations as described in \secref{applicability-with-special-params}.
Therefore, static parameters, keyword parameters, and varargs parameters are
ignored in the remainder of this chapter.
\end{quote}
The sentences added to \secref{resolving-coercion}, after the Working Draft's
lines 455--459, 522--524 and 567--570 of
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/conversions-coercions.tex}, and the new
section have no counterpart there.
The new section, the revival's text of 30~September 2026, stated:
\begin{quote}

171	
172	**Peers, measured.**
173	- Java 25 refuses `class O implements A, B` (abstract `pick` in A, default in B): "O is not abstract and does not override abstract method pick() in A".
174	- The tree's Scala 2.13.18:
175	  - accepts O and the narrower-return O2, which print `b` and `r1`;

178	
179	### 2.1 Specification
180	
181	**Passages that bend.**
182	- **The override and inheritance definitions** (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:661-667`, or `:573-579`) need one more case: in a trait or object, an abstract method declaration that it inherits is overridden by a method definition that it inherits from another immediate supertrait with:
183	  - the same name;
184	  - the self parameter at the same position;
185	  - the same parameter type, the self parameter's apart;
186	  - an equal return type (or, for Scala's full rule, a subtype).
187	
188	  With that case:
189	  - inheritance (`:575-576`, "except those … overridden") and "provides" (`:580-581`) both leave `A.pick` out of what O provides;
190	  - the abstract-method rule (`:628-633`) and `objects.tex:154` then find no inherited abstract method;
191	  - `objects.tex:149-151` already reads this way: "must include a definition for every method declared but not defined by its supertraits".
192	- **The choice at a call.** Functional applicability is by parameter types alone (`basic/overloading.tex:191-201`). So `A.pick` stays applicable to `pick(O)` beside `B.pick`, and neither is more specific. Today the Meet Rule makes O provide a meet, so the static call has a most specific declaration. Under the change no meet is required, and the static call has none. A sentence is needed, and the text already has it as a draft-only note (`traits.tex:653-655`): "Method declarations that are overridden by some declaration are not accessible." Made normative, as "not applicable to a call whose self argument's type does not provide it", this lets `B.pick` choose the call's type. The compiled checker already types `pick(O)` as `R1` (measured). The run-time rule of an arbitrary maximal declaration (`basic/overloading.tex:309-312`) then chooses between declarations that reach one definition.
193	- **Appendix I.** An entry and its `\revision` callouts, in the P-96 form.
194	
195	**Unchanged.** The Meet Rule's wording (`advanced/overloading.tex:417-430` and `:469-485`) stays, because O no longer provides both declarations. P-147's coverage rule is satisfied under both readings: the team's abstract-method check counts inherited bodies (`AbstractMethodChecker.scala:94-107`, team lines).
196	
197	**Under reading (a)** no normative sentence changes. Under both readings the Appendix I effect sentence at `changes.tex:2622-2627` ("reads no abstract functional method of a trait that the component it checks declares (row 727)") becomes half false.
198	
199	**The type group's later word.**
200	- **Welterweight (2012, the calculus behind P-147)** refuses O:
201	  - `D-Object` checks Meet over `allVisible(O)` (`fig-wellformeddecls.tick:66-81`), which takes every method of every ancestor, abstract ones included (`fig-miscjudgments.tick:77-82`);
202	  - a method's domain includes its declaring type (`fig-msa.tick:52`);
203	  - so no third declaration is equivalent to `A ⊓ B` (`Meet-Third`, `fig-meetrule.tick:56`);
204	  - its `Covered` rule alone would accept O.
205	- **POPL 2019** has no abstract declarations (`ParkPOPL2019-extract.md:328`), so it is silent.
206	- **The Dispatch paper** (Steele, Chase, Allen, Luchangco and Ryu, POPL 2011 submission):
207	  - abstract declarations require objects that inherit them "directly or indirectly" to provide matching definitions (`Papers/Dispatch/body.tick:169-171`);
208	  - its implementation turns `f` with self at `j` into a dotted `f$j` plus a top-level forwarding function (`:1607-1650`), the scheme both implementations follow;
209	  - under that scheme the run time has no ambiguity for O.
210	- **The team's later restart** (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/overloading.tick:24`, `:45`): the run time picks among definitions; the rules promise a unique most specific declaration at compile time. That second promise is the part that needs the call-choice sentence above.
211	
212	### 2.2 Checker
213	
214	**The smallest rule.** Reading (a) at `:139-141`, plus one exemption beside `implemented` (`:151-156`): drop an abstract functional method that the type provides beside a body c when:
215	- c's declaring type is not at or below the abstract one's;
216	- the self position is the same;
217	- `oracle.equiv` holds on both domains without self;
218	- the return types are equal (both directions of `returnBelow`, read as `checkOverridingReturnType` reads them).
219	
220	For consistency, the same filter goes on the dotted set at `:387`. That is a team line; without it the dotted twin stays refused while the functional one is accepted. The variants are listed under Method above.
221	
222	**It still refuses:**
223	- row 727, where the declaring type is the same;
224	- two sibling bodies;
225	- an abstract method beside a sibling body with another return type;
226	- two abstract declarations met in a type with none of its own. Scala accepts this last shape; walk refuses it today.
227	
228	**It is local:**
229	- it fires 0 times over the count stage, RangeInternals and the distance stage;
230	- the compiler's library compiles with no firing;
231	- the `scala2`+`cg` suites match the `lifted` ones: CompilerJUTest has only the row 727 flip, LibraryJUTest has 86 OK, OtherCompilerJUTest has 263 OK.
232	
233	**Two caveats.**
234	- The `scala` variants change 16–18 class files of CompilerBuiltin and 7 of CompilerLibrary, though the exemption never fires there. Only the order of an overload dispatcher's tests between excluding cases changes; for example, `CompilerBuiltin$Unordered`'s SQCAP tests the arrow type before or after `Comparison`. This is F-232 and row 488 territory. `lifted` alone and `cg` alone leave the jars byte-identical.
235	- Bodies in an imported api are invisible to the rule as built, because an api's index has no bodies. An api declaration without the `abstract` modifier would have to be read as a body.
236	
237	### 2.3 Walk
238	
239	**Why it refuses today.** It does not stop at the call. Since 833420ce4 (F-142), the per-provider Meet check refuses at load (`OverloadedFunction.java:1148-1162`): "Invalid overloading of pick in O: O provides the functional methods pick(self) of A and pick(self) of B …".
240	
241	**What lies beneath.** The object's method table keeps the first declaration of each signature in extends order (`Constructor.java:182-183`, `putIfAbsent` at `:846`, `:854` and `:859`). I ran a shadow with only the Meet exemption:
242	- `extends { A, B }` is then refused by `checkForDef` (`:425-452`): "Object O does not define an abstract method declared in type A";
243	- `extends { B, A }` runs `b`.
244	
245	The old internal error at the call (`MethodClosure.java:88`) is no longer reached by this shape.
246	
247	**The smallest fix, two local edits:**
248	1. In `Constructor`, a body takes the place of an abstract declaration of the same signature whatever the extends order, when its return type is at or below the abstract one's.
249	2. In `FunctionalMethodMeets.check` (`:1156`), a pair of an abstract declaration and a sibling body that implements it needs no meet.
250	
251	**Evidence.** SystemJUTest with the shadow ran 621 tests. It failed the same two, ReflectTest and ReflectiveQuickCheckTest, as the base does in one JVM with the same seed (`1a13ddfc5c1_16`). Both pass alone, at 1 and at 4 threads, on the base and on the shadow.
252	
253	### 2.4 Code generator
254	
255	**With equal return types it already runs B's body for every call form.** Calls typed by O, A and B, through `viaA` and `viaB`, with self second, through trait Z, and on the generic instance all print `b`.
256	
257	**With a narrower body return type it does not.** Every call dies with AbstractMethodError, `pick(O)` included: O has no method with A's descriptor.
258	- A bridge in `dumpMethodChaining` (an object only, mirroring how `dumpOverloadedMethodChaining` narrows an object's own declaration) fixes the dispatch: `r1` ×3.
259	- `o1: R1 = pick(O)` still fails to load. The checker types the call `R1`, but the code generator compiles A's declaration (`R`): "Type R is not assignable to R1". That fix belongs in the code generator's choice of the declaration at a call; I did not prototype it.
260	
261	**Across an api boundary, two defects that exist today and that valid programs reach (rows below):**
262	- A body inherited from an api trait that is not first in the extends clause is never forwarded, because `dumpMethodChaining` skips declarations without a body (`CodeGen.java:965`).
263	- An api trait first, plus a same-named method in a later trait, crashes the compile, "Not in the trait table" (`CodeGen.java:1006`). It crashes even for a valid overloading of `tag(self, n: ZZ32)` and `tag(self, s: String)`, which walk runs and prints `cd`.
264	
265	## 3. The smallest clean resolution
266	
267	**Scala's way for equal parameter and return types, within a component:**
268

270	|---|---|
271	| checker | reading (a) plus one exemption, and the dotted twin if the two forms are to agree |
272	| walk | two edits |
273	| code generator | none |
274	| specification | the override case and the normative non-accessibility sentence, plus Appendix I |
275	
276	Measured: no other program's result changes, the library never triggers it, and rows 727 and 572 close the way Scala closes them.
277	
278	It reaches further in three directions:
279	- covariant returns: the code generator's static call choice;
280	- api boundaries: two code-generator rows;
281	- two abstract siblings: a further rule that Scala has and the minimal rule does not.
282	
283	Reading (a) remains one condition with no change to the specification. It agrees with the type group's calculus, with Java and with the specification's letter.
